title: Quantum Dynamics of $H_2^+$ in Orthogonal Two-Color Fields
abstract: We present full-dimensional quantum simulations of $H_2^+$ dissociative ionization driven by strong orthogonal laser fields. We consider equal-frequency orthogonal components, which generate elliptical or circular polarization depending on their relative phase and amplitude, as well as orthogonal $800$- and $400$-nm two-color fields. These two-dimensional fields strongly modify the fragmentation dynamics. Most notably, we identify a high-energy peak in the proton kinetic-energy-release (KER) spectrum at approximately $4-5$ eV that is absent from the corresponding single-color, linearly polarized calculations. The yield of this peak can be coherently controlled by varying the relative carrier-envelope phase of the perpendicular field component. The perpendicular field also disrupts the clear electron-proton energy-sharing pattern observed in the main $3-3.5$ eV dissociation channel, indicating more complex multichannel dynamics. Time-dependent state projections and calculations initiated from individual excited states attribute the additional peak to laser-induced vibrational excitation of $H_2^+$. Furthermore, the perpendicular field rotates the fragment angular distributions, causing the most probable proton and electron emission directions to deviate substantially from the principal $z$ axis. These findings demonstrate that the spatial and temporal geometry of orthogonal laser fields provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling ultrafast electron-nuclear dynamics.
summary: The paper simulates the dissociation of H2+ driven by strong orthogonal laser fields to understand ultrafast quantum dynamics. Key findings include the emergence of an additional high-energy proton peak, which is controllable via the relative phase between the field components. This demonstrates that the spatial geometry of multi-dimensional laser fields offers a powerful new degree of freedom for controlling molecular fragmentation.
main_problem: The study investigates the quantum dynamics of H2+ dissociative ionization when driven by strong, orthogonal laser fields.
main_result: Orthogonal fields introduce a high-energy proton kinetic-energy-release (KER) peak ($\approx 4-5$ eV) absent in single-color calculations, and allow coherent control over this yield via the relative carrier-envelope phase.
method: The research employs full-dimensional quantum simulations using time-dependent methods to calculate Joint Energy Spectra (JES) for dissociative ionization.
model_or_system: The system is the hydrogen molecular ion (H2+), modeled with a Hamiltonian including electronic, nuclear, and electron-proton interaction terms. The dynamics are driven by intense laser fields composed of orthogonal components ($\vec{E}(t) = E_z(t)\hat{z} + E_x(t)\hat{x}$).
key_observables: Proton Kinetic-Energy-Release (KER) spectrum, electron–proton energy-sharing pattern, and fragment angular distributions.
important_parameters: Laser field geometry (orthogonal components), relative carrier-envelope phase ($\phi$), and pulse duration/frequency (e.g., 800-nm, cos^8 pulses).
main_assumptions: The simulation uses the tSurff method, which assumes neglect of particle interactions beyond large radii; full-dimensional simulations are computationally demanding.
figures_summary: Figures compare JES under linear vs. circular polarization, show the dependence of a secondary KER peak yield on the relative phase ($\phi$), and illustrate how angular distributions rotate with field phase for short pulses.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using full-dimensional quantum simulations to model H2+ ionization. It then presents results comparing single-color vs. orthogonal fields, highlighting the secondary peak generation, and finally discusses the control mechanisms afforded by varying the relative phase of the perpendicular field component.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics in molecular physics using intense laser fields, providing detailed insights into how field geometry (spatial/temporal) acts as a control knob for electron-nuclear energy partitioning and fragmentation pathways.

In the DI region, both the nuclei and the electron have crossed their respective tSurff surfaces. Here, R(+) c and R(−) c are the tSurff radii associated with r1 = |⃗r1| and r2 = |⃗r2|, respectively.
